reviews.text: Sadly, yet another promising shoot em up ruined by trying to be half shoot em up, half roguelite slop em up, and not particularly good at either. The main problem revolves around the upgrade system - it's an advancing selector system like Gradius, but it misses a couple of bits central to the design that make that game work. Number one, unlike Gradius, you don't get to control where upgrades spawn, only when. They can get pushed under level geometry or enemies with absolutely 0 possibility of getting them back, or the map itself can suddenly switch making them unobtainable. Number two, it has an absolutely punishing power curve, where falling even a couple of upgrade tokens behind is a run-ender. There's no way to push back ahead of the curve and play more skillfully, there's no version of this game where you're alive at all if you don't get more or less all of the speed upgrades very early into a run. The game itself seems to realise this is a shonky system and gives you multiple upgrade cards to pull glimmer (the xp currency) and upgrade tokens at longer ranges, or even across the map, and the game is reasonably fun with those. Trouble is - you have absolutely no control over when those spawn, either. It's basically mashing a deterministic remember 'em up kind of game like Gradius into a sloppy who cares game like Vampire Survivors, only without the predictability of the former, or the persistent upgrades of the latter. In a committed slop em up, the XP/token attractors would be in a permanent upgrades page. Unfortunately this game wants more than anything to be taken seriously as a scoreboard shooter, so it doesn't quite have the courage to go there. It does not really work out that well. The urge to make a hiscore shooter completely trips over the urge to make it a roguelite, and it ends up not being very good at either. Your runs get cut short by stuff you could never have controlled, and your high scores are just a list of the runs where you got something that pulled upgrades out from the walls the game plonked over them at random. If you're looking for something combining bullet hell, boss rush and roguelites that doesn't tragically misunderstand all the genres involved, The Void Rains Upon Her Heart is what you're after instead.

[quote] 《SEKTORI》是一款画面简约其貌不扬，但是玩上了就非常上头的双摇杆射击游戏。它把快节奏的弹幕战斗和硬核科技音乐狠狠揉在一起，打造出一种近乎癫狂的沉浸体验——你操控简约三角飞船在枪林弹雨中穿梭，耳边是pounding的电子节拍，眼前是色彩炸裂的光效与弹道（不过太花了也有点不好，后期经常看不到敌我弹幕）。游戏有多种模式供玩家游玩，每种模式都有特色，并且还有排行榜。 游戏操作很简单，你只需要学会控制方向、射击以及冲刺，就已经掌握了本作所有操作。游戏共有七种模式，初始的战役模式、经典、涌动、星门、冲击、强袭以及头目连战，后面几种模式都需要达到评分条件才会解锁。战役模式非常像类幸存者模式，需要击败敌人拾取经验升级然后强化自身； https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3610225557 经典模式则是典型的打怪升级刷分，不过有一个变因元素，可以增加/降低难度，比如增加/减少敌人耐久（不同的变因需要达成对应条件才会解锁），但是变因之后就不会保存分数；涌动模式，和经典模式类似，但没有升级系统，拾取闪标直接进入火力全开属性拉满的状态； https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3610226057 星门模式就很有趣了，摒弃了射击和冲刺系统，你只能通过穿过蓝色星门触发爆炸击杀敌人得分；冲击模式则是舍弃了射击系统，换来了能够多次冲击，冲击得分闪标会触发大范围爆炸来解决敌人；强袭模式，更具挑战的一个模式，敌人分波次袭来，开启波次的权力在你自己手里，稳中求稳可以一波一波应对，对操作够自信可以一次性开启数波敌人；而最后的头目连战，就是和你解锁过的Boss进行连战。个人最喜欢的其实是战役模式，其他模式都太过于“单纯”，战役模式有五个动态变化的世界，加上“变革”难度下堪称变态的挑战，让你每一局都面临全新考验。 https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3610225576 并且局外还可以DIY你的飞机以及进局里的卡组，飞机种类不多，但是个性鲜明，比如初始飞机救赎号均衡、反叛号火力弱但是冲刺次数多等等。除此之外，局内也有不少随机事件，比如击败精英敌人获得抽卡机会、凑齐毁灭字母迎来彩虹时刻等等。 从视觉到听觉，这游戏都贯彻着科技音乐的美学灵魂：高饱和的色彩、凌厉的线条、迅猛的节奏，仿佛一场持续不断的感官轰炸。如果你喜欢在枪林弹雨中思考，又渴望那种全心投入、忘记时间的“心流”状态，那么本作绝对能让你爽到。 [quote] 游玩百态，将游玩心得用汉语化作玩家的指明灯，(๑•̀ㅂ•́)و✧ [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/35402408/]点击这里关注汉化语录~[/url] 如果喜欢这个评测，请点个赞让更多人看见 [/quote] [/quote]

Also the bosses are incredibly tedious to fight - every single one of them is a bland invincible structure with massive hurtboxes you have to weave through to hit glowing spots, which is simply not fun and is pretty much the only time you'll take damage. Could have been much better and could still be improved, but probably won't because it's already attracted the weird gitgud crowd.

I sit down on my flight next to an older man, probably in his 70s or 80s. He whips out his phone and boots up Mahjong. I smirk, smirkingly. He has no clue what’s coming. I give him a generous 15 minutes to get his bearings with me, his seat mate, to let him acclimate and enter his own flow state. My hands find the soft case containing a near-stock LCD steam deck - just some after market thumbsticks and rear grip pads to enhance comfort. I unzip Sheila from her case and depress the power button. Sheila instantly snaps on to the simplistic, yet aesthetic, main menu of Sektori, the music lightly thumping. In a swift, practiced motion, I mute my steam deck and connect my headphones. I wanted to flex on the Air Force veteran to my left, not give him a heart attack, after all. Seizures, now, those I wouldn’t be able to prevent. I start the Campaign on the easiest difficulty and the first few minutes fly by. My ship sends volley after volley of purple missiles to collide with geometric shapes made up of pixelated fireworks. I spell out “MIRAGE” and Sheila turns into a rainbow of color and destruction. I enter into a flow state where I bring order to chaos. My weapon is a stream of prismatic energy cutting through waves of enemies as if I had turned on a firehose against some birthday candles. Up until this point, I had never beaten the fourth boss. I maxed out all the upgrades. I felt a glimmer of the power that gods wield. And I cannot wait to step into the zone again, searching for the upgrade token as deliberately as my seat mate searches for his two matching Mahjong pieces. I never spoke to my seat mate, or looked in his direction for a reaction to what could only be described as a dichotomy of gaming intensity. But as we were stepping off the plane, I swear I heard him mumble something to himself. “Sek to reye, huh?”

A lot of negative reviews are focusing solely on difficulty, so I'll try to address why I think Sektori is needlessly difficult. I'm going to focus exclusively on campaign, because the less random Arcade modes are more balanced imo. I'm not going to claim that anything is impossibly hard, only that some of the difficulty is due to some frustrating design decisions. The following elements actively getting in the way of players using the tools meant to overcome the increasing challenges of a run. Upgrades: Tracking whether or not you've got enough points to buy an upgrade requires glancing away from the action or counting in your head. In a game where decisions happen in fractions of seconds, this means the UI causes frustrating deaths. They could instead either add a simple indicator somewhere center screen (you learn the upgrade order quickly) or better yet, have the voice that announces the chosen upgrade instead announce the level you've reached. I don't need to be told I just bought missiles, I would love to be told I reached that upgrade level. Strike: This is clearly meant to be a central mechanic given the token synergy and score multiplier. I have read many people talking about taking the upgrades last and deprioritizing the related decks. It creates complete visual chaos which sometimes leads to an enemy or bullet blindsiding you after the strike. The recharge indicator is difficult or impossible to see even if I'm staring at my ship (you can crank the visibility of the line, but it's still not where I want to be looking). In a game of this style I rarely look at my ship. I am scanning for a safe path and targets. The ship is, at best, in my peripheral vision. A steady sound, a background hue, or some other very obvious indicator might work better. Also just my .02, but a small vacuum effect for points at the strike location would make a huge difference in how it feels. Building a perfect path of 10+ strikes only to be unable to collect any of the points feels terrible. Which leads me to: Level rotation: I get it. it adds to the chaos, but it has never once felt challenging when the level swaps to separated areas with no fully connected teleport path only to switch to more separate cells with no path at all. I have lost many tokens and points this way while sitting, bored, waiting for the action to start again. It breaks the flow and takes away player choice. Similarly having the level change to a configuration that completely blocks them before the ships from an objective even enter the screen just sucks. Decks: I won't go into why some decks are good or bad, I'm sure that could be debated. However, Challenge and up starts to really punish you for taking legendary cards to the point that it's often better to skip them unless you've mastered the game. The glaring example is losing your shields for large portions of time. For most players, carefully balancing the choice of buying more shields vs upgrades that increase power is how we survive a run. Suddenly losing the benefit of the shields I've carefully maintained or accumulated is rarely worth the risk. That means I'm being punished for getting lucky. It's a rug pull moment that feels bad. The upgrades often aren't good enough to warrant the risk which brings me to: when a card with a mediocre rare perk is presented as rare I effectively have one less option rather than an exciting better option. It also makes Rare Imports suicide for most players. The game at its core _is_ fun. The problem is that past Experience, it's not. Most people just aren't going to enjoy it past the first difficulty so I can't recommend it in its current state.

The best twin-stick shooter since Nex Machina, thereby cementing Finland as the capital of GOAT twin-stick shooters. What impresses me the most is that it's actually an arcade game disguised as a roguelite, instead of the other way around like usual. Recently we have been getting more arcade-y games like Absolum that try to modernize arcade gameplay with roguelite (meta-)progression systems and randomized level design, but these often end up lost in the sauce and become more about numbers and builds the deeper you get into them. Sektori somehow strikes a perfect balance: it has all the pros of roguelite elements and none of the negatives. It has all the run variation and unpredictability you'd expect of a roguelite, but without outright ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ RNG or the progression systems overpowering the core gameplay. Plus, you can unlock almost everything within three hours of playing. This was inevitably done by reducing how much influence the progression elements have on the gameplay, meaning that you're going to be disappointed if you're the kind of player that likes devising overpowered builds. But for the kind of gameplay that Sektori is going for, I'd say it is a net positive. And unlike most arcade games, Sektori isn't the kind of game that you need to bust open a Practice Mode for to practice stages individually. Hell, it doesn't even have a Practice Mode. It's basically unthinkable for any modern arcade shmup/beat 'em up release to not include some kind of practice mode or stage select, but in Sektori it's absence is barely even felt. Outside of the boss fights, there are no massive difficulty spikes or difficult parts that you would need to memorize, nor would it even make sense to do so with its randomized boss order and arena order. This really is a game that you can just keep getting better at by just playing it instead of practicing it like you're doing homework. The scoring and more randomized aspects ensure that replaying the first few stages remains fresh on repeat playthroughs, but there are still enough unique stage layouts and new enemy types regularly being introduced to make each stage feel distinct. That said, the boss fights do have some "tricks" to their attack patterns that take some time to really understand (like figuring out how to move through the spinny ring boss' rings), and that is exactly where having a more robust boss select would have come in handy. The existing Boss Rush mode comes close to doing that, but it doesn't let you practice bosses individually. Even more impressive is that despite the heavy emphasis on unpredictability and controlled injections of RNG, is that Sektori has a competitively worthwhile scoring system. It is actually highly unusual for an arcade game to do so; newer arcade games (shmups in particular) are rather scared of adding RNG, because RNG tends to not mix well their scoring systems. Basically, there's little point to high score chasing on the leaderboards if how high your score is might depend heavily on luck. The way Sektori pulls this off is that it gives you a lot of means to mitigate the randomness. Most of its scoring comes down to regularly dashing into tokens to keep up a multiplier, but the spawn position of tokens is random. Sometimes a token might be out of reach, or in a part of the arena that is about to change, but you can then mitigate this by keeping a surplus of multiple tokens on the field, instead of picking up every token as soon as possible. So if you can't reach a token in time before your multiplier decays, then you always have other tokens to dash into as a backup. Of course, tokens quickly despawn if not picked up long enough, so you can't build up a ridiculously big surplus either. At the same time there are other pressures at play: sometimes you are about to get overwhelmed by enemies, and sometimes it might pay to dash into a token sooner than intended, as doing so also briefly boosts your rate-of-fire and clears out all enemies/bullets around you. Sometimes your dash is on cooldown right when you need to pick up a token, but you can instantly recharge your dash cooldown by purchasing an upgrade as a sort of fallback, even if your currently selected upgrade isn't the one you currently wanted. It's one beautiful well-oiled machine. Every function serves multiple purposes, and every goal has multiple competing and contradicting goals, where figuring out how to thread the needle to satisfy each one is the satisfying part. It's never 100% clear what is the most optimal way to play, and that is what keeps Sektori fresh on each run. The implementation of the randomness isn't 100% perfect -- there are some randomly chosen areas here and there where it's basically impossible to keep your chain and multiplier going -- but it's good enough. I love this game so much, because it's useful to learn from for arcade and action roguelite games both. For arcade games it shows how to tactfully implement unpredictability with a worthwhile scoring system, and for action roguelites it shows that you don't really need to double down on RPG elements to have run variety. Truly, a best of both worlds.

This is an addictive arcade style game with surprising depth and several different modes. I've played a lot of arcade games from every era, and while this resembles a few of them on the surface, I haven't seen one that is quite like Sektori. The changing shape of the arena is the main attraction, but it's actually only a fraction of what you need to be paying attention to. Don't be fooled by the "deck builder" mechanic in the game. This isn't another rogue-like. The deck is specific to each run, and it doesn't introduce the kind of RNG to suppress raw skill and artificially inflate your play time. EDIT: This may be the culmination of decades of arcade games. This is the greatest arcade game ever made.

Sektori is swiftly becoming one of my favorite games of all time. It is a hectic, overstimulating rush of focus and energy. This game feeds off of my ADHD, and behind that veil presents the single most unbelievably difficult twin stick shooter I've ever played. Every death feels like my fault, every hit you take teaches you something if you're willing to look. The bosses are amazing (wowie great boss fights in a twin stick shooter???). You have so many paths to modify your build using the deck/card system and stack upgrades. You have a damaging dash attack with i-frames, but this isn't a crutch; it is built into the combat and enemy design, and it is integral to scoring well. This game looks like a kaleidoscope yet could not be clearer to see what's happening; it sounds like a hard techno rave with outstanding sfx, yet it's mixed well enough to easily hear important cues. The menus, bosses, background, even the FLOOR beats with the music. This game is such a treat to play!! Don't disregard the warnings within the difficulty settings. Experience may be the easiest mode, but it'll still put up a fight. Challenge may be the "intended" difficulty, but it's called Challenge for a reason. Revolution... turns this game into one of the hardest bullet hell/avoidance/horde management games i have EVER played. I just recently got my first win on revolution difficulty... at 110 HOURS of gameplay lmao. The game also has six alternate gamemodes that help teach you the fundamentals of the mechanics. Each is fairly short but gets brutal quickly. All seven gamemodes have an intricately designed scoring system. Everything has its own leaderboard. I bought the soundtrack alongside the game, and i wish i could buy it again to throw more money at the devs. Selling this game for 15 USD feels like I'm stealing lol.
